# Flygon Flow

> Flygon Flow keeps a MindMap (people, entities and ideas; called charts in the API), a product timeline, a DevOps board and AgentFlow (agents and workflows) in one workspace per environment. People use the web app. Agents use the same operations through the REST API, the MCP server or the CLI, authenticated with a personal API key (`flow_…`).

Releases: `GET /api/devlog` on your Flow server (one per production deploy), also in the app under Settings › DevLog.

# Concepts

## Environments

An **environment** is one workspace: its charts, projects, timeline and DevOps board, plus a record of who owns it.

```json
{"id": "acme-hq", "name": "Acme HQ", "ownerEmail": "owner@example.com", "visibility": "private", "members": []}
```

- Every user starts in a new, empty, private environment. They can create more, rename them and archive them from Settings › Environment. Archiving hides an environment and keeps its data.
- **Isolation.** A private environment can only be seen by its owner and its members. Anyone else gets `404`, so the server does not even confirm that it exists. Anyone signed in can read a public environment, but only its owner can write to it.
- Every API operation that touches workspace data is scoped to one environment through the `{env}` path segment. The server runs the read or write check before it touches any data.
- Data saved before environments existed belongs to the instance's default environment.

## MindMap (charts)

The app's **MindMap** tab is a free-form canvas of **cards** joined by **edges**. The API calls each mind map a **chart** (`charts.list`, `nodes.*`, `edges.*`). A workspace can hold several charts; one of them is active. In the app, right-clicking a card, a connection or empty canvas opens a menu of the actions that apply there.

- Card types: `entity` (a company or organisation), `person`, `area` (a project area that groups cards inside it) and `note`.
- Edge types: `ownership` is a solid arrow that can carry a percentage from 0 to 100, or `""` when the percentage is unknown. `group` is a dotted line that means grouping only.
- Cards snap to a 16px grid and can be resized. Moving an area also moves every card that sits fully inside it.
- A `person` card can have a **photo** (`image`: an `https://` URL, or a `data:image/png|jpeg|webp;base64,` URL of at most 61,440 characters) and an **email** (`email`, up to 200 characters, stored lower-case). In the app, the person's side panel can upload a photo (cropped to a 128px square), remove it, or **Use my photo** to take your account photo and email. A person whose email is yours shows your account photo until they get one of their own; so does a person with no email who is the only person in the workspace with your account name (matched ignoring case and extra spaces). **This is me** (shown when you are signed in and the person has no email) sets their email to yours, so they keep showing your live account photo. Matching only changes what is displayed: nothing is saved until you choose one of these buttons. The photo then appears wherever that person does: their card, DevOps assignee bubbles, pickers and AgentFlow supervisor badges. Invalid values, and photos or emails on other card types, are dropped.
- Sharing a person shares their photo with whoever can see the card, but never their email.
- Selecting an entity or area shows its **project strip**: the projects placed under it, their next timeline item, backlog counts and open DevOps cards.

```json
{"id": "c1", "name": "Acme · structure",
 "nodes": [{"id": "acme", "name": "Acme Holdings", "type": "entity", "x": 400, "y": 0},
           {"id": "rivera", "name": "Sam Rivera", "type": "person", "x": 320, "y": 144}],
 "edges": [{"id": "o1", "from": "rivera", "to": "acme", "type": "ownership", "percent": "60"}]}
```

Validation is strict: ids must be unique, every edge must join two existing cards, and a card cannot connect to itself.

## Timeline

The timeline holds dated **items** that are tagged with **projects**.

- Item kinds: `feature`, `milestone`, `release`, `deadline`, `project`, `phase`, `event`.
- Status: `planned`, `active`, `risk`, `blocked`, `done`, `cancelled`. Priority (`high`, `medium`, `low`) is optional.
- `start` is `YYYY-MM-DD`, or empty for an unscheduled backlog item that appears only on the Board and List views. `end` is optional and never earlier than `start`.
- A feature can target a **release** by title. The release then lists the items that target it and how many of them are done.
- **Projects** are coloured tags `{id, name, color, entity}`. A project can sit under a chart entity or area through `entity`.
- Done and cancelled items turn grey and fade in every view, and the toolbar can hide them.
- When all of an open item's linked cards are done, Flow suggests marking it complete. It never closes the item itself.
- Views: Timeline (Gantt), Calendar, List and Board (a kanban by status). Filtered items can be exported as `.ics`.

## DevOps board and gates

The DevOps board is a card board. Each card has an auto-incrementing `#number`.

Columns, in order: `requests` (Requests / Sprinted, where new cards land), `doing`, `blocked`, `uat`, `done`, then the two backlogs `must` (Must Have) and `nice` (Nice to Have).

A card holds `title, description, column, project, labels[], points, actual, due, assignees[{node, role}], checklist[{text, done}], links[{kind, url}], item` and the `created` / `updated` / `moved` timestamps. Assignee roles are `developer`, `tester` and `requester`, and each assignee is a person card on the chart. Link kinds are `pr`, `commit` and `url`. `item` links the card to a timeline item. `points` is the estimate made up front and `actual` the points the card actually took, recorded after the work (for example from the agents' token use); both are a number from 0 to 1000 or null, and setting one never changes the other. Responses also list `agents`, the AgentFlow agents the card is delegated to (see AgentFlow: delegation and the work queue).

### Gates

Some moves need a confirmation or a decision. The app asks for it, and API callers must provide it explicitly:

| Move | Gate |
| --- | --- |
| UAT → Done with **Approve** | none (approval is the gate) |
| anything else → `done` | `confirm-done` |
| `done` → anything | `confirm-reopen` (reopen) |
| → `doing` with no developer | `pick-dev`: choose who develops it |

Labels have a section (`priority`, `urgency`, `area`, `topic`, `other`) and a colour key. Due dates turn amber two days before they are due and red once they are overdue.

### Recently deleted

Every card that leaves the board is recorded on the server first, whatever removed it: **Delete** on the board, undo or redo, a snapshot restore or other whole-workspace save from a browser, or the API and MCP. The record holds the whole card as it was, who removed it (`deletedBy`; `via`: `board`, `undo`, `snapshot`, `save` for a tab running older code, `api`, `mcp`; and `actor`, the API key's name), when, the last revision it was in (`fromRev`) and the environment. Records are kept for 180 days, apart from the revision history, so a card can be restored long after its revision has rolled off.

`cards.deleted` lists them, newest first (`q`: `#12` or title text; `pending: true` leaves out restored ones). `cards.restore` puts one back with the same id, column, fields and agent links. It keeps its number unless another card has taken it; then it gets the next number, `renumbered` is `true` and `message` says so. In the app, the ↺ button in the board's toolbar opens **Recently deleted**, with a Restore button per card.

A save that removes cards without a Delete (an undo, a restored snapshot) still goes through, so the other changes in it are not lost; the answer lists them as `removedCards`, and the app says they can be restored from Recently deleted. A save from an older revision is refused with `409` as before, and the browser merges it, which keeps cards added meanwhile.

### Snoozing cards

A card can be snoozed until a time: the clock button on the card (shown on hover or focus) or its right-click menu offers In 1 hour, In 3 hours, Tomorrow (9:00 AM), Next week (Monday 9:00 AM) and Custom… (a date and time), each with the time it lands on. The snooze is the card's, stored as `snoozedUntil` (an ISO time) and the same for everyone on the board. Until then the card is left out of its column; the clock in the column header shows how many cards there are snoozed and shows or hides them (dimmed, with their wake time), remembered per column for each person. The toolbar's card count leaves snoozed cards out; when any are snoozed, a clock beside it shows how many and shows or hides them in every column at once. An agent's work queue (`agents.work`) leaves them out too. When the time passes the card is a normal card again, with no job on the server: the board works it out from the time. Moving a snoozed card keeps its snooze. Through the API and MCP, `cards.update` takes `snoozedUntil` (an ISO time, or `""` / `null` to wake it; a past time wakes it too), `cards.get` and `cards.list` return it (`null` when awake), and `cards.list` takes `snoozed: true` or `false` to keep only snoozed or only awake cards.

### Board order and column sorts

Board order is the order of the cards in the board (`cards.list` returns it); dragging a card within a column changes it. In the app, each column header has a sort menu: Manual (board order), newest or oldest first, recently updated, due date, points, actual points, priority (Urgency labels, then Priority labels, in the order they are listed) or card number and title. A sort is a view for one person: it is kept in their preferences, never in the workspace, and it does not change the board order or any card. Cards missing the sorted value (no due date, no points, no actual points, no priority label) go last, and ties keep board order. Reordering inside a sorted column is refused until it is back on Manual; moving a card into a sorted column puts it at the end of the board order.

## Agent inbox

Agents can add or update projects, labels, timeline items and cards by dropping a JSON **patch** into the inbox. The open app picks the patch up within about 20 seconds and merges it as **one undoable step**.

```json
{"source": "Claude", "env": "acme-hq", "ops": [
  {"op": "upsertProject", "name": "Launch", "color": "#7cb980"},
  {"op": "upsertCard", "title": "Write release notes", "project": "Launch", "column": "requests", "labels": ["High"]},
  {"op": "patchCard", "number": 12, "column": "uat"}
]}
```

- Ops: `upsertProject`, `upsertLabel`, `upsertItem`, `upsertCard`, `patchCard`.
- References use names: a project by name, an assignee by the name of a person card, an item or release by title, and a label by id or name.
- **Safety:** ops only add or update and never delete. Lists only grow. A field a human changed after the patch was written is kept, and the merge notes it. Applying the same patch again changes nothing.
- CLI: `node tools/inbox.mjs add|check|list|requeue`.

The token API is the direct way to make changes. The inbox suits agents that cannot hold a token, or changes a human should be able to undo in one click.

## Sync

The server is the source of truth. Each environment's workspace is stored with a **revision** number, and the browser keeps an offline cache.

- `GET /api/workspace?env=<id>` returns `{rev, data}`. `PUT` with `{baseRev, data}` saves the workspace when `baseRev` is still current.
- If the workspace has moved on, the save gets `409` along with the newer copy. The client then merges per entity and field and retries. When both sides changed the same field, the local change wins. A deletion only applies to an entity the other side has not touched.
- DevOps cards are the exception: the board never sends its copy of them as edits. It keeps a list of the cards it changed itself (`cardEdits`: the fields it changed and what they were before, the cards it added and removed), and the server writes only those. Every other card stays as the server has it, so a copy that is out of date (a tab that slept, a browser that could not store its latest copy) never puts old descriptions, columns or due dates back on cards that an agent or another tab changed. When it was out of date on some cards, the answer includes `cardsKept: true` and the client reads the workspace again. An edit over a value the browser never saw (someone else changed that field meanwhile) gets `409` with `code: "card_conflict"`, the clashing cards and the newer copy; the browser shows it, keeps the user's edit and says so. A tab still running an older version of Flow that would change cards gets `428` (`reload_required`) and has to reload.
- A save that would drop most of a large workspace is refused with `422`, unless it is a deliberate load or replace.
- AgentFlow runners belong to the server: only `runners.report` changes them. A `PUT` keeps the runners as they last reported (their models and scheduled jobs), even when the saved copy is missing them or holds an older report, such as a tab still running an older version of Flow. The answer then includes `runnersKept: true`, and the client reads the workspace again.
- Card numbers only grow. A `PUT` with a lower `devops.nextNumber` keeps the server's and answers `countersKept: true`, so the client reads the workspace back.
- Every write first keeps the previous revision in the history. Postgres keeps it in `flygon_flow_workspace_history`; without Postgres it goes to `BACKUP_DIR/workspaces/history/`. The last 100 revisions are kept.
- A write that removes DevOps cards also records each card in `flygon_flow_card_deletes` (or `BACKUP_DIR/workspaces/deleted/`), in the same transaction, for 180 days (see Recently deleted on the DevOps board). A `PUT` may send `intent: {deleted: [card ids deleted on purpose], undo: true|false}` so the record says how each card left; other removed cards come back as `removedCards`.
- Open tabs pick up remote changes every 20 seconds, and offline edits upload when the connection comes back.

API writes go through the same revision check, so an agent's change and a human's edit never silently overwrite each other. An agent that reads a card and writes it back (for example, adding to its description) can send `ifUpdated` with the card's `updated` to `cards.update` or `cards.move`; if the card changed since, nothing is written and it gets `409 card_changed` with the current card.

## Sharing

The owner of an environment can share part of it with another Flow user, by email: a person and everything below them, hand-picked cards, a project, a DevOps label, or the whole environment. The Share dialog (a card's **Share…** button, or Settings › Environment › *Share this environment…*) shows a live preview of exactly what the other person will see. Permissions are **view**, **comment** or **edit**.

The recipient finds it under Settings › Sharing › *Shared with you* and adds it to one of their own environments. The shared cards appear there as linked boxes with their own layout. Direct co-owners of a shared card show as read-only name stubs, and nothing else of theirs is shared. Edits travel both ways as the permission allows. Shared timeline items and DevOps cards carry the same link badge and name their owner, and fields the permission does not allow are locked. A shared card can be assigned to its share's members: the owner and the people it is shared with. If two people change the same field at once, the last change wins, and the person whose change was replaced sees "Changed by … just now" on that field, with the previous value and a one-click restore. Revoking a share removes everything from the recipient's environment. Recipients cannot share further; instead they ask the owner, who approves or denies the request.

A whole environment shared with you can also be **opened** as itself: it is listed in the account menu and Settings › Environment as "<environment> · shared by <owner>" with your permission, and opening it shows the owner's charts, timeline, DevOps board and AgentFlow as they have them, so you work in the same place. What you may change is what the share allows. AgentFlow agents and workflows come along too; an edit share can change their design and delegate cards, while an agent's Live switch, runner, models, schedule, instructions and tools stay with the owner, because they decide what runs on the owner's machines. Its 3D office is the owner's office, so everyone it is shared with meets there. When the share is revoked, the app says so and opens your own workspace.

The server enforces all of this: linked copies are computed from the owner's data on every read and are never stored in the recipient's environment. API keys and MCP see the shares placed in your own environments the same way, with the same permissions. The owner token used by the CLI sees each environment's own stored data only. Details: `docs/sharing.md`.

Anyone with a OneProfileID account can join Flow, and members can invite friends to the app itself (Settings › Account › *Invite to Flow*). A new person gets their own empty environment and sees nothing of anyone else's until it is shared with them.

## Versioning

Flygon Flow uses [Bradshaw Versioning](https://github.com/aribradshaw/devlog/blob/main/docs/bradshaw-versioning.md) numbers. Every production deploy gets the next `YEAR.MONTH.UPDATE`:

- The year is zero-based from 2026, so October 2026 is `0.10.x` and January 2027 is `1.1.x`. Months are calendar months, in the America/Phoenix timezone.
- One release per deploy. A release lists every commit the deploy brought, plus `compatibility` (`compatible`, `action-required` or `breaking`, with the required `action`).
- The server records the release when the deploy starts. Nothing is committed back to the repository.
- `public/devlog.json` is the frozen history from before deploy releases (up to `0.11.25`).

The app's Settings › DevLog and `GET /api/devlog` list every release, newest first.

## AgentFlow

AgentFlow is an org chart for agentic work. You lay out the agents that do work for a business, say what each one is for and what it takes in and produces, chain them into workflows, and tie them to the projects, DevOps cards and deadlines they own.

Flow stores the design. It does not run agents itself. A runner of your choice (an agent harness, a home server, a cron job) reads an agent's or workflow's **brief** through the API or MCP and does the work, then reports back on the DevOps cards like anyone else.

### Agents

An agent has `name, kind, title, status, live, reportsTo, supervisor, purpose, instructions, runtime, models[], model, auto, schedule, inputs[], outputs[], tools[]`, an optional `job`, and links `projects[], cards[], items[]`.

- `kind`: `agent` (an AI agent), `human`, `team` (a group heading in the org) or `automation` (a scripted job without AI, such as a backup timer, that runs on its own schedule outside Flow; see [Automations](#automations)).
- `schedule` says when it runs, in plain words or cron, such as "Weekdays 09:00" or `30 22 * * *` (`""` for none). For an AI agent it is a note carried in the brief: the reference runner works by Live and its queue, and does not start work from it.
- `job` is `{runner, id}`: the runner job it was promoted from (see [Scheduled jobs](#scheduled-jobs)). It is absent when there is none; send `null` or `""` to `agents.update` to clear it.
- `status`: `draft`, `active`, `paused` or `retired`.
- `reportsTo` is another agent. Together these form the AgentFlow org chart. An agent cannot report to itself or to anyone below it (`reports_loop`). A saved loop is broken when the workspace loads.
- `supervisor` is a person card on one of your mind maps: the human accountable for the agent. A `human` agent shows a person's photo: its supervisor's, else that of the only person card with the agent's name, else your account photo when the agent has your account name and no person card does.
- `inputs`, `outputs` and `tools` are short text lists, such as "A card in Doing" or "Pull request linked on the card".
- `instructions` holds the system prompt or runbook. `runtime` says where it runs (a runner's name).
- `models` lists the models it may run on, up to 10 ids from its runner, in order: the **primary** first, then **fallbacks** the runner tries when one fails (a rate or usage limit, a provider that is down). `model` is always the first of them, kept for older runners; sending `model` alone to `agents.update` sets `models` to just it, and when both are sent `models` wins.
- `auto` turns `models` into a pool: the runner picks one per card instead of always starting on the first. The org card shows **Auto (N models)**, or the primary model and **+N** for its fallbacks.
- `live` is the switch runners obey. It is off for every new agent, and a runner leaves an agent that is not live alone, whatever its status. Turn it on in the agent's side panel, or with `agents.update` (`live: true`). The org card then shows a **Live** badge, in amber when its runner would skip it (no runner or model picked, or a model its runner did not report).
- Deleting an agent moves its direct reports up to its manager, and its workflow steps become unassigned.

### Runners

A runner is a machine or service that runs agents, such as a home server with agent harnesses installed. It tells Flow what it can run with `runners.report`: its name and the models it offers, each with an id, a label and optionally a `provider` to group it under (such as "Claude" or "OpenCode") and `billing`: `included` (covered by a subscription, or free) or `metered` (paid per use). `runners.list` returns them. In an agent's side panel, **Runs on** suggests the reported runners and **Models** that runner's models, and every org card shows where the agent runs and on which model. Reporting the same models again saves nothing, so a runner can report on every pass.

```sh
flow runners report --input '{"runner":"Home server","models":[{"id":"claudeAgent:claude-sonnet-5-5","label":"Claude · Sonnet 5.5","provider":"Claude","billing":"included"}]}'
```

`tools/agent-runner.mjs` is a reference runner for [T3 Code](https://t3.codes): it reports the providers and models signed in on its machine, and for each live agent whose `runtime` is its name, starts a T3 thread on the agent's model for the top card in its queue (Doing, then Requests), moves the card into Doing as the thread starts, and moves it to UAT when the thread finishes. Doing means an agent is working the card now: on every pass, a card in a live agent's queue that sits in Doing with no thread running for it (waiting for a free slot, say) goes back to the top of Requests, and a thread waiting on a question keeps its card in Doing. If a model will not start, or its thread fails or hits a limit, it starts the card again on the next model and keeps every attempt; when all have failed, or the thread is interrupted or cancelled in T3, it moves the card to Blocked (`retry <number>` puts it back in Requests). For an `auto` agent it prefers `included` models over `metered` ones, keeping the pool's order, and can ask a small "router" model to choose among the included ones from the card and the agent's purpose. It marks Claude, Codex, Cursor, Grok and Antigravity models `included`, OpenCode's own free models (`opencode/…`) `included` and other OpenCode models `metered`, and its settings can override that. It starts in dry-run mode, so it only prints what it would do until you turn that off. See the comment at the top of the file for its settings.

### Scheduled jobs

A runner can also tell Flow which scheduled jobs it found: systemd timers, crontab lines, scheduled T3, Claude or Aside tasks, Codex automations, Vercel or Railway crons, GitHub Actions schedules, Windows scheduled tasks. It sends them as `jobs` in the same `runners.report` call, up to 500 per runner:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `id` | Required, up to 200 characters, stable per runner, e.g. `systemd:backup.timer` or `vercel:my-app:/api/cron/sync`. |
| `name` | Up to 120 characters (defaults to the id). |
| `source` | Where it is scheduled, up to 40 characters: `systemd`, `cron`, `t3`, `vercel`, `railway`, `aside`, `windows`, `claude`, `codex`, `github` or `other` (the default). Other text is kept as it is. |
| `group` | A display group, up to 120 characters, e.g. "Home server" or "Vercel · my-app". |
| `schedule` | When, in words, up to 200 characters: "Daily 22:30", "Every 5 min". |
| `cron` | The cron expression, when there is one (up to 120). |
| `timezone` | The zone its times are in, up to 64 characters: an IANA name such as `America/Phoenix`, `UTC`, or `local` (the runner's own zone; see below). |
| `triggers` | Every rule it fires on, up to 10: `{kind, expr, text}`. `kind` is `cron`, `calendar` (a calendar rule such as a systemd `OnCalendar` line or a daily or weekly Windows trigger), `interval`, `logon`, `boot`, `once`, `rrule` (RFC 5545), `manual` or `other`; `expr` is the raw expression as the scheduler holds it (up to 200), such as `*/5 * * * *`, `Mon *-*-* 09:00:00` or `OnUnitActiveSec=5min`; `text` is it in words (up to 200). |
| `origin` | Where the schedule was read: `repo` (a config file in a repo), `platform` (the hosting platform's API) or `machine` (the machine's own scheduler). |
| `file` | The repo-relative path of the config it came from (up to 200), such as `services/worker/railway.json`. |
| `drift` | How the platform's live schedule differs from the repo file, when it does (up to 200). |
| `note` | Conditions the job's script applies itself, such as "Exits early when nothing changed" (up to 500). |
| `command` | A short summary of what it runs (up to 300). |
| `ai` | `true` when the job starts an AI agent. |
| `enabled` | `false` when it is switched off on the runner (default `true`). |
| `lastRun`, `nextRun` | ISO times. |
| `lastStatus` | `ok`, `failed`, `running` or `unknown` (the default). |

The report can also say the runner machine's `timezone` (an IANA name), which jobs with `timezone: "local"` are in; left out, the stored one stays. `jobs` replaces the stored list. Leave it out to keep the stored jobs, or send `[]` to clear them. `models` is optional too: leave it out to keep the stored models, as a runner does when it reports the jobs of another machine it reaches over SSH. To keep writes down, a report is not saved when the only changes are `lastRun` and `nextRun`, unless the jobs were last saved six hours ago or more. A changed `lastStatus`, a job added or removed, or any other field (a new trigger, drift or note) always saves. The runner's `jobsReported` is when its jobs were last saved, and the response's `changed` says whether this report was.

```sh
flow runners report --input '{"runner":"Home server","models":[],"timezone":"America/Phoenix","jobs":[{"id":"systemd:backup.timer","name":"Nightly backup","source":"systemd","group":"Home server","schedule":"Daily 22:30","timezone":"America/Phoenix","triggers":[{"kind":"calendar","expr":"*-*-* 22:30:00","text":"Daily 22:30"}],"origin":"machine","command":"restic backup /srv","lastStatus":"ok","lastRun":"2026-11-02T05:30:00Z","nextRun":"2026-11-03T05:30:00Z"}]}'
```

In the app, **Scheduled** in the org chart's toolbar opens a tray on the left of the canvas. It lists every runner's jobs by runner and group, each with its source icon, name, schedule and a dot for the last run (green OK, red failed, grey unknown). Hover the dot for the last and next run. A row names the time zone (such as `UTC`) only when it is not yours and the schedule has a time of day, and shows an amber dot when the schedule has drifted from its repo file. Click a row, or its **i**, for the job's details: the schedule in words, every trigger with its raw expression, the time zone (always named; a `local` job shows its runner's zone), where it was read (**Repo file** with the file's path, **Platform** or **Machine**), drift in amber, the note, the command, the last run and its status, the next run (when, in your time and the job's zone), whether it starts an AI agent and whether it is enabled. **Promote to org** is there too. Escape or a click elsewhere closes it. A group with more than eight jobs starts collapsed to a chip such as "59 jobs" that opens it. Search filters the tray too. Whether the tray is open, and which groups you opened or closed, is remembered on this device.

The reference runner (`tools/agent-runner.mjs`) reports the jobs it finds with every `report` and `tick`: systemd user and system timers (stock distribution timers such as apt-daily, fstrim and logrotate are skipped), the user's crontab, T3 scheduled tasks (read only from T3's database; needs Node 22.5+ for `node:sqlite`), and cron configs in your repos: `vercel.json` crons, `cronSchedule` in `railway.json`/`railway.toml`, and `on.schedule` in GitHub Actions workflows. Repos default to your T3 projects' folders. Commands are summarised on one line with anything that looks like a secret hidden. Every job comes with its full schedule: its `timezone` (this machine's zone, from `timedatectl` or Node; the zone an `OnCalendar` line names; a crontab's `CRON_TZ`; UTC for repo crons), its `triggers` (each `OnCalendar` line as a calendar trigger, `OnUnitActiveSec` as an interval and `OnBootSec` as boot; each crontab line; T3's schedule as T3 holds it), its `origin`, and for repo crons the `file`. Run `node tools/agent-runner.mjs jobs` (or `jobs --json`, with every field) to see the list without contacting Flow; the table has **TZ** and **ORIGIN** columns, and `!` after the origin marks drift. Tune it with `"jobs"` in `runner.json`: `sources`, `repos`, `exclude`, `include` (keeps a job even when `skipDistro` or `exclude` would drop it), `skipDistro` and `notes`; `"jobs": false` stops reporting jobs and leaves the stored list as it is.

**Notes.** For a Railway cron, the runner reads the README in the service's folder (else its start command's script, and for a Vercel cron its route's source) and takes the first sentence that says it runs every N minutes, exits, or applies a condition ("only when", "unless", "unchanged", "skips", "does not run"), plus the first condition after it when both fit in 200 characters. It never uses a sentence that mentions a token, secret, password or credential, and hides anything that looks like one. `"notes": {"<job id or name>": "text"}` in `"jobs"` (globs or substrings, first match) wins; `""` removes a note.

**Platform schedules.** A repo file says what should run; the platform says what does. With a token, the runner reads the live cron schedules and matches them to the repo's cron configs:

- `railwayToken` (or `RAILWAY_API_TOKEN`): every service's cron schedule and next run from Railway's GraphQL API, matched to `railway.json` configs by service name (`railwayWorkspace` picks a workspace's projects).
- `vercelToken` (or `VERCEL_TOKEN`): each project's crons from Vercel's API, matched to `vercel.json` by the folder's `.vercel/project.json` link, else by project name (`vercelTeam`, a team id or slug, for team projects).

A matched job is reported as the platform runs it (origin `platform`, with its `file` kept) and its next run from the platform, and `drift` says how the file differs, such as "Railway runs `*/10 * * * *` (Every 10 min); services/worker/railway.json has `*/5 * * * *` (Every 5 min)", or that the platform has no cron for it. A live cron that no repo file has is reported too. Without a token nothing is asked; `"platform": false` in `"jobs"` turns it off. Put tokens only in your own `runner.json` (or the environment), never in a repo.

#### Remote machines

The reference runner can also read the scheduled jobs of other machines over SSH, such as a Windows laptop, and report each one as a runner of its own, named after it. It sends that runner's `jobs` only, so the remote shows in the Scheduled tray (and its jobs can be promoted) without any models. List them as `"remotes"` in `runner.json`:

```json
"remotes": [{"name": "Laptop", "ssh": ["ssh", "-i", "~/.ssh/laptop_key", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "me@laptop"],
             "python": "C:\\Python\\python.exe", "timezone": "America/Phoenix"}]
```

- `ssh` is the ssh command as a list, ending with the host. Use a key and `BatchMode=yes` so it never asks for a password. The remote's login shell may be `cmd.exe`: the runner sends its scripts on stdin, PowerShell through `powershell -EncodedCommand`, and Python when `python` (the path to `python.exe` on the remote) is set. Both scripts only read.
- `timezone` is the remote's time zone (an IANA name). Its cron lines and schedules are read in that zone, and its jobs and runner report it. It defaults to the runner's own.
- `sources` picks what to read (all by default):
  - `windows`: Task Scheduler tasks outside `\Microsoft\`, with their triggers in words ("Daily 18:00", "Every 15 min", "At logon", "On demand") and each trigger's raw settings (its type, start, days and repetition, such as `TimeTrigger, start 2026-10-15T08:51:32-07:00, repeat PT15M`), last and next run, and status from the last result. Vendor updater tasks (Adobe, Edge, Google, Zoom, McAfee, HP, OneDrive and so on) are skipped unless `skipVendor` is `false` or `include` names them.
  - `aside`: Aside routines, active and paused (`keepDone` adds completed ones). Each shows its schedule from its RRULE (one-shots as "Once Nov 1 18:00"; the raw rule and its TZID are its trigger and zone), its model and prompt, and its last run. A routine waiting for approval shows as running, with "Waiting for approval". One whose next run has already passed is marked "(stale)". Needs `python`: Aside's database is copied to a temporary folder, read and removed.
  - `claude-desktop`: Claude desktop scheduled tasks, with what each one does taken from its `SKILL.md`.
  - `codex`: Codex automations, from their RRULE or cron line and status. One-shots whose runs are used up are skipped (`keepDone` keeps them, marked "(done)"). With `python`, the last run of each cron automation comes from Codex's database.
  - `vercel`, `railway`, `github`: cron configs in the repos listed in `repos` (paths on the remote).
- `include`, `exclude` and `notes` work as in `"jobs"`. `timeout` is in seconds for the whole remote (40 by default), and `enabled: false` turns a remote off.

`tick` reads the remotes after its own pass, at most every 15 minutes, and keeps the time in its state file. `report` reads them every time. A remote that cannot be reached is logged and tried again next time, after one retry if the connection fails, and it never holds up the local pass. Run `node tools/agent-runner.mjs jobs --remote Laptop` to see a remote's jobs without contacting Flow, or `jobs --all` for this machine and every remote.

#### Promoting a job

To put a job in the org, do one of these:

- Drag the job onto an agent's card. It becomes that agent's report.
- Drag it onto empty canvas to place it at the top level, right there.
- Click **Promote** on the row (top level).
- Right-click it and choose **Promote to org**, or **Promote under** the selected agent.

The new agent is selected and its side panel opens. Undo removes it again. A job without AI becomes an **automation**, and an `ai` job becomes an AI agent whose `runtime` is the runner (pick its models, then switch it to Live). Either way the agent is named after the job, its role comes from the source (such as "Vercel cron" or "systemd timer"), its `schedule` is the job's (or its cron line), its purpose is the command, and its status is Active, or Paused when the job is disabled. It is never live, and `job` links it back. A job is promoted once: its row then shows **Promoted** (click it to select the agent), and promoting it again selects the agent it already became.

### Automations

An automation (`kind: "automation"`) is a scripted job in the org with no AI in it. It runs on its own schedule, outside Flow, so it has no runner, no models and no Live switch: `live` is always false, and a runner never works it. Its card is shorter and grey, with a gear, and shows its schedule (and its job's last status) where an AI agent's card shows its runner and model. Its side panel has a **Schedule** section with the schedule, and, when it came from a runner job, the same details as the Scheduled tray shows for it under **Promoted from**: triggers with their raw expressions, time zone, origin and file, drift, note, command, last and next run (read-only, as the runner reports them). An AI agent's `schedule` is under **Runs on**, and its card shows a small clock when it has one.

The brief lists `Schedule: …` and `Promoted from: <runner> · <job name>` under Runtime.

### Workflows

A workflow has `name, description, status, trigger, schedule, steps[{agent, action, output}]` and the same links. `trigger` is `manual`, `schedule` or `event`. `schedule` says when or on what in plain words, e.g. "Weekdays at 09:00" or "A card enters UAT". Steps run in order, and each one names the agent that handles it.

### Delegation and the work queue

Delegating a DevOps card to an agent puts it in that agent's **work queue**. The person on the card stays accountable; the agent does the work. Delegate in the card's **Delegated to** picker, from the agent's side panel (Cards), or with `cards.update` (`agents: ["Researcher"]`; `[]` clears it). Cards show their agents as square badges, and the board's **Agents** filter shows one agent's cards. A card can be delegated to several agents.

`agents.work` returns everything a runner needs in one call: the agent, its brief, and its queue, which holds the open delegated cards. The queue is ordered Doing, Requests / Sprinted, Blocked, UAT, then the backlogs, and by soonest due date and `#number` within each. `columns: ["doing","requests"]` keeps only the cards it can act on now. A snoozed card stays delegated but is left out of the queue until its snooze ends, then comes back on its own (`includeSnoozed: true` keeps snoozed cards in); the brief marks it snoozed. A runner loop on any machine looks like this:

1. `agents.work` with the agent's name and `columns: ["doing","requests"]`.
2. Take the first card. Move it to Doing with `cards.move` if it is new.
3. Do the work, following the brief and the card's description and checklist.
4. Report back with `cards.update` (tick the checklist, add the pull request under `links`), then `cards.move` to `uat` for a human to approve.

A runner only works agents with `live` on: `agents.list` with `live: true` gives it that list.

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLOW_TOKEN" "$FLOW_URL/api/v1/envs/$FLOW_ENV/agents/Researcher/work?columns=doing,requests"
flow agents work --input '{"agent":"Researcher","columns":["doing","requests"]}'   # or the agents_work MCP tool
```

The runner only calls out to Flow and never needs to be reachable itself, so it works from a home server behind a router.

#### Seats in the 3D office

In the [3D office](#3d-office), each AgentFlow agent has a desk in the common area: the agent is the job, and a live coding session working on one of its cards is the one doing it, seated at its desk. The reference runner names its T3 threads `[Flow] <Agent>: #<n> <card title>`, which is enough for the office to seat them. Any other runner or reporter can say it outright with `agentflow: {agent: "<agent id or name>", card: <card number or id>}` on the session in `office.agents.report`; without it, a `#<n>` in the session's title seats it when that card is delegated to exactly one agent. An agent's desk panel lists who is at it now, the first five cards of its queue and the cards it finished in the last seven days. See [Seats](#seats) for the rules and who sees what.

### Briefs

`agents.get` and `workflows.get` return a `brief`: Markdown with everything a runner needs. That covers purpose, reporting line, inputs, outputs, tools, runtime, workflow steps, linked projects, cards (open ones from linked projects too) and deadlines, and the instructions. In the app, **Copy brief** in the side panel puts the same text on the clipboard.

### In the app

The AgentFlow tab has two views: **Org chart** (`1`) and **Workflows** (`2`). **Scheduled** opens the tray of runner jobs (see [Scheduled jobs](#scheduled-jobs)). The org chart is a canvas like the MindMap: drag empty space to pan, scroll to zoom, drag a card to move it (Shift: with its reports), and drag the dot under a card onto another agent to make that agent report to it, or onto empty space to add a new report. Each AI agent's card shows small icons for the makers of its models in the bottom-right corner (the primary first, then up to two fallbacks and "+N"), or one auto symbol with a count when it is on Auto, and its supervisor's face sits on the corner of its avatar. Double-click empty space to add an agent. **Tidy up** returns to the automatic tree. In the tree, a manager's reports that have no reports of their own are stacked in indented columns (up to six per column) once there are three or more, so a large team stays compact and no reporting lines cross. Positions are saved as the agent's optional `x` and `y`. An agent without them, such as one added through the API, is placed under its manager, below the last of its teammates. `N` adds an agent under the selected one, `W` adds a workflow, `/` searches, `F` fits the org, arrow keys nudge the selected agent. Right-click (or the menu key) opens a menu on an agent, a reporting line, a workflow card or empty canvas: change kind, status or manager, add the agent to a workflow, open its work queue on the DevOps board, duplicate a workflow, and so on. **Start from a template** creates a small example org and workflow to edit. A DevOps card's detail shows the agents linked to it, and you can assign agents from there.

## OneProfileID photos

When Flow runs with OneProfileID sign-in, a person card can show that person's current OneProfileID account photo, for everyone who can see the card. The person links the card themselves; Flow never links a card to an account because an email address or a name matches.

- **Link a card.** Open a person card whose email is your sign-in email and choose **Link to my OneProfileID** in its side panel. This works on cards in your own environment and on person cards shared with you at any permission. A card without your email can't be linked; add your email to it first (that needs edit access). From then on the card shows your current account photo, and it updates when you change your photo in OneProfileID.
- **Unlink.** You can always unlink your own account. Anyone who can edit the card (its environment's owner, or a recipient of an **edit** share) can also choose **Unlink** on a card linked to someone else. Changing or removing a linked card's email unlinks it too, from the app, the API or MCP, so a link never follows a card that now names someone else.
- **API and MCP.** Cards show `opidUser` (read only) to the environment's owner, and only `opidLinked` to anyone else. Linking happens only in the app, by the person themselves: API keys, MCP and the owner token can't add a link.
- **Which photo shows.** A linked card shows its account photo first. An uploaded photo is the fallback while the account has none, and a card with neither shows initials. Cards that are not linked work as before.
- **Who is shown.** A linked photo is looked up only for people who have opened that environment with OneProfileID, as its owner or through a share, and who still have access. OneProfileID applies its own rules as well. Photos are fetched when Flow opens and when its window regains focus, cached for a minute, and never saved into the workspace or its history.
- **Who sees the link.** Only the environment's owner sees which account a card is linked to. Share recipients and other readers see that a card is linked, and see their own link. The link is stored as `opidUser` (the OneProfileID account id) on the person card.
- **The server enforces it.** On every save (the app, the API, the CLI and MCP) a new or changed `opidUser` is kept only when it is the saving person's own OneProfileID account id; anything else is refused and the previous value stays. A duplicated card is never linked. API keys and the owner token can keep or remove links but never add one. In local single-user mode there is nothing to link.

## Chat

With OneProfileID sign-in, a chat bubble in the bottom right corner of Flow lets you message your OneProfileID friends without leaving Flow, and send them Flow cards. It is the same conversation as the Messages bubble on the OneProfileID website: what you send here shows there, and the other way round.

- **Who you can message.** Your friends: people you follow on OneProfileID who follow you back. **New message** (the pencil) lists them, with people you already talk to first. OneProfileID checks the friendship on every request.
- **When it shows.** Only with OneProfileID sign-in, and only once OneProfileID has turned messages on for this Flow. In local single-user mode, or before then, there is no chat bubble at all.
- **Send a card.** On a DevOps card, choose **Send in chat** in its detail view, or right-click the card. On the MindMap, right-click a card (or use its side panel) and choose **Send in chat**. You can also drag a DevOps card onto the open chat or onto the bubble. Pick a friend if no conversation is open, add a note if you like, and send.
- **What is sent.** Messages are plain text. A card goes as a readable title line and a link to the card on this Flow, for example `Flow card #12: Fix the sign-in loop` followed by `https://flow.example.com/?env=<environment id>&card=<card id>` (MindMap cards use `node=<id>`). On the OneProfileID website it stays readable as that text and link. A card shared with you links to its owner's card, so everyone who gets the link opens it with their own access.
- **How a card shows.** In Flow, a message that links to a card on this Flow shows as a card: its title, number, column, labels, project colour and assignees, or a person's photo for a person card. The details are looked up for the person reading, with their own access: from the environment they have open when the card is there, otherwise through the server, with the same rules as opening the environment or a share. Someone who can't see the card sees only the title the message carries, with "You don't have access to this card". Nothing else about the card reaches them, not even whether it still exists.
- **Open a card.** Click a card in a conversation, or open its link. Flow opens the environment it belongs to for you (your own, one you may read, or the environment where you placed its share) and shows the card. A card from a share you haven't placed in one of your environments asks you to add the share first (Settings › Sharing).
- **Polling.** The conversation list refreshes every 15 seconds while it shows, an open conversation every 5 seconds, and the unread badge every minute, only while the Flow tab is visible.
- **Privacy.** Flow sends OneProfileID only your own OneProfileID session from this browser, so messages always go out as you. The chat routes take no user, email or account id, and the only other person they ever name is a friend's handle. Messages are not stored in Flow.

## Combined view

The DevOps board and the Timeline can show several of your environments at once. Open the account menu (top right): each of your other environments has a box beside its name. Tick it to show that environment's cards, timeline items and projects in the one you have open. Clicking the name still switches to it. The menu and the toolbars then say **Combined: N environments**, and a legend under the toolbar names each environment; its × stops showing it. Your choice is kept with your preferences, on every device you sign in on.

The environment you have open stays the home: new cards, items and projects go there, and the mind map and AgentFlow show it alone. Each card and item from another environment carries a small badge with that environment's name, and keeps its own number (so two cards can both be #1). Shares placed in a combined environment come along too, with their own permissions: a view-only share stays read-only.

Edits to a card or item from another environment go back to that environment, never into the one you have open: title, description, column (moves on the board), points, due date, labels, assignees, checklist, links and snooze for cards; title, kind, status, priority, dates, owner, link, notes and target release for timeline items; name and colour for projects. Deleting it, adding to it, giving it another project or timeline item, or delegating it to an AgentFlow agent is done in its own environment. The combined environments are read again whenever any of them changes, at the same 20-second interval and on returning to the tab as the rest of the workspace. Details: `docs/combined.md`.

## 3D office

The 3D office is a small virtual office for one environment, where you can see your team and the coding agents they have running right now. Open it from the AgentFlow toolbar with **3D** (between **Workflow** and **+**). It fills the window; **Esc** or the close button takes you back to AgentFlow.

To link straight to it, add `#office` to Flow's address (`https://your-flow.example/#office`): Flow opens AgentFlow and then the office, after sign-in and once the workspace has loaded. `#office/<id>` also opens one agent's panel: a live agent's id as its reporter sends it (`homebox:t3:abc`; URL-encode anything unusual), or an AgentFlow agent's id or name. Closing the office takes the address back to `#agentflow`.

- **Rooms.** Every member of the environment has a room with their name plate beside the door (which also says when they are away and whether agents are running): the environment's owner, and everyone with an active share into it (see [Sharing](#sharing)). A room is dimmed, with when its member was last here, while they don't have the office open. The common area in the middle holds the environment's AgentFlow org, laid out like the org chart: AI agents are small robots, teams round tables, automations little machines, and people are people. Their names show when you are near, hover or select one. Click one to see it, or to open it in AgentFlow. A human agent that is one of the members (matched by its person card's email, else by name) is that member's avatar while they are here, and stands at its place in the org, dimmed and marked offline, while they are not.
- **The DevOps board.** The main board, on its own feature wall in the ring of rooms, is your DevOps board itself: the same board as the **DevOps** tab, live, not a copy. Walk up and press **E**, or click it, and the camera turns to face it; it then works exactly as in the tab: open a card (it opens over the office), right-click menus, snooze, drag cards between columns, filters, search, sort, undo and the DevOps shortcuts. While you work on it the office's walking keys pause. **Esc**, **Back to office** or a click beside the board takes you back. Its title is the office's environment, and starts with **This office ▸** when doors connect the office to others. It shows the board of the environment you have open, so in an office you visit from your own environment it says so, and offers to open that environment's board when it is shared with you as a whole (Flow then opens that environment, as the environment menu does, and the office again there).
- **Room whiteboards.** Each room's back wall has a whiteboard with that person's cards in Doing, UAT and Blocked, in board order, each with its count, its first cards and how many more there are. Cards show their number, title, project colour and who is on them (people as round dots, AgentFlow agents as square ones). From far away a board shows only its title and counts. Walk up to a whiteboard and click a card to open its DevOps details, or press E to open the first card in the lane in front of you. Left-drag a card onto a person or room to add a developer, onto another whiteboard column to move it, or onto an AgentFlow agent in your workspace to add it to that agent's queue. Hold **Shift** while dropping onto an agent to replace its current delegates. Use **Undo** in the confirmation to reverse the latest drop. On the DevOps board, the card's right-click menu has **Assign developer** and **Delegate to agent** for the same. An agent with a Doing card shows its number beside its name. The room boards use the cards available in your workspace, including cards shared with you in the office you visit.
- **Meters.** A small screen by each room's door, and one beside the main board, shows agents running and waiting, cards shipped today, points shipped this week, and a 24 hour sparkline. The office screen also shows how many of your own agents are waiting on you. Walk up and press **E** for the details. See [Meters](#meters).
- **Live agents.** The coding agents running on a member's machines sit at desks in their room, as a little mascot: Claude's crab, a cloud for OpenAI and Codex, a whale for DeepSeek, Grok's black sphere, Gemini's sparkle, or an orb for anything else. Its subagents are tiny copies circling it. Click an agent (or its name tag) for its title, model, machine, repo and project, what it is doing and its subagents.
- **Seats.** The AgentFlow agents are the jobs; a live session working on one of an agent's cards is the one doing it. It sits at that agent's desk in the common area instead of a desk in its owner's room, as the same live mascot, with the agent's name and the card (such as **Builder · #12**) on its tag. An agent with nobody at its desk stands idle and dimmed. Click an agent for who is at its desk now, its queue (the first five cards, as `agents.work` orders them) and the cards it finished (moved to UAT or Done) in the last seven days. Allow and Deny still go only to the session's owner. See [Seats](#seats) for how a session finds its desk.
- **What they are doing.** A running agent acts out its kind of work (its [`activityKind`](#activity-kinds)), and its name tag starts with the matching sign: it types at its keyboard while it edits files (✏️), reads a floating book (📖), sweeps a magnifying glass while it searches (🔍), has terminal glyphs on its screen while it runs commands (⌨️), shakes a bubbling test tube that flashes green and red while it tests (🧪), thinks under a thought cloud (💭) or spins a little globe on the web (🌐). An idle agent is dim, and goes about the office calmly (☕): a while at its desk, at the coffee corner, in front of the board or a few steps away, 10 to 40 seconds at each, and now and then two idle ones meet and chat, with a small "…" over them.
- **Everyone walks.** Agents, AgentFlow robots and offline people move like people in a game: they walk along real paths, through doors and around desks, walls and each other (and you), and never jump from place to place. A new session comes in at its owner's room door (one seated at an AgentFlow desk, at the edge of the common area) and walks to its desk and sits down. A session that ends stands up, waves, walks out and fades. A session that gets seated walks from its room to the AgentFlow desk, and back when it is unseated. When a session picks up a new card it walks to the board, takes the card and carries it to its desk; when its card moves to UAT or Done it carries it to the board, puts it up and celebrates. Subagents trail behind their agent while it walks and circle it while it is still. When the office is laid out again (someone joins, the org changes), everyone walks to their new place, or fades over when it is far. Robots with nobody at their desk wander about the common area, and someone who just left the office walks from where they were to their place in the org. What each one does is chosen from its id and what the server says about it (status, kind of work, seat, card), so everyone in the office sees much the same scene.
- **Waiting gets your attention.** When an agent starts waiting on its person (⏳), it glows with a **!** and, if its owner is in the office, walks over to their avatar and hops beside them until it is answered, then walks back to its desk. If its owner is not in the office, it hops at its desk. For the owner, it also plays a short, soft ping; the speaker button in the office's top bar turns the sound off and on. Click the agent or its **!** for its panel, with **Allow** and **Deny** when the prompt can be answered from Flow.
- **Alerts outside the office.** Turn on **Notify me when agents wait** (the bell in the office's top bar). Then, while Flow is open in any tab with the office closed, each time one of your own agents starts waiting your browser shows a notification (the browser asks for permission once), and the **3D** button shows how many of your agents wait. Clicking the notification opens the office on that agent. Only you are alerted about your agents: never anyone else, even people who can see the agent's project. The setting is remembered with your preferences; turn it off with the same button.
- **Transcript.** Your own agent's panel shows the latest lines of its conversation (up to 12: what you asked, what it said, and one line per tool call), scrolled to the newest. Only you ever see it: not the environment's owner, not someone who can see its project. Reporters mask secrets before sending, and Flow masks tokens, keys, `Authorization` headers and `.env`-looking lines again on the way in.
- **Send to agent and Stop.** When its reporter can carry them out (T3 Code threads, through `flow office bridge` or another reporter that says so), your own agent's panel has a **Send to agent** box and a **Stop** button. Type a message and press **Enter** to send it (**Shift+Enter** for a new line): it reaches the agent as your next message, after its current turn when it is busy. **Stop** asks you to confirm, then interrupts its running turn. Each one shows as sending, then sent (waiting for the reporter), then how it went. While you type in the box, the movement and shortcut keys go to the box, not the office. Only the agent's owner ever gets these, they are rate-limited, and the reporter checks the agent is still the same before it acts. Claude Code in a terminal cannot be reached from outside, so its panel has neither.
- **Allow and Deny.** When your own agent waits on a permission prompt that its reporter can answer, its panel shows the prompt with **Allow** and **Deny**. Your answer goes to the reporter on that machine (usually within a second), and the panel shows how it went. Only the agent's owner ever gets these buttons. The agent nods (or shakes its head for Deny) the moment you click, and works with a few gold sparks over it until the answer is through; everyone in the office sees it react, never the prompt. The panel says **Approved** or **Denied** at once, **Running…** when the agent's next report has it working again, and the reporter's message in red if it did not go through. If nothing comes back in 20 seconds it says **Still waiting on** its machine.
- **People.** Everyone who has the office open is an avatar with a name tag (and their account photo when they have one). Each person has a look: a face, hair, an outfit and shoes. Until you choose one, yours is picked for you and stays the same every visit. See [Your look](#your-look).
- **Press E.** Walk up to an agent, a person or a board and a prompt says what **E** does there ("E Talk to Chief of Staff", "E Wave at Joe"); on a gamepad it is X / Square, and on a touch screen you tap the prompt. E again, Esc or walking away closes what it opened. The camera turns with **Z** and **C**.
- **Status.** Each person sets Available, Focus, Do not disturb or Away. It shows on their avatar, name tag and door sign. See [Status](#status).
- **Meeting room and voice.** A glass meeting room has its own place in the ring of rooms. Walk in to join its call: the first time, the browser asks to use your microphone. Everyone in the room hears everyone else, and walking out leaves the call. The sign at its door says who is in it ("Live: 3 in Meeting room"), and a green ring under an avatar shows who is speaking. Outside the room, **Talk to people nearby** in the voice bar (bottom right) lets you hear people within about 6 m who also have it on. Their voices get quieter with distance and come from their side. See [Voice](#voice).
- **Screen sharing.** In the meeting room, **Share screen** in the voice bar (or **E** at the table) shows your screen on the room's wall screen for everyone in the call. Click the wall screen, press **E** in front of it, or use the expand button to watch it full screen. One screen is shared at a time: if someone else is sharing, Flow asks before yours replaces theirs.
- **Knocking.** Someone else's room has a door. You walk in when they are available, away, or not here. Focus and Do not disturb keep it shut until they let you in. See [Knocking](#knocking).
- **Chat and emotes.** Type in the box at the bottom left (or press **T**). The channel chip shows who will get your message. See [Chat channels](#chat-channels). Wave, thumbs up, clap and heart are the buttons beside it, or keys **1** to **4**. Click someone's avatar to wave, follow them (until you move yourself) or start a message to them.
- **Worlds.** The office can be the classic **Office** or a **Yacht**. See [Worlds](#worlds).
- **Several offices.** If shares from other people's environments are placed in yours, the office's title becomes a menu: pick a shared environment to enter its office as a member. The shared office opens first, until you pick another.
- **One office for a shared environment.** When you open an environment shared with you as a whole (see [Sharing](#sharing)), its 3D office is the owner environment's office: the same rooms, the same chat and the same people, so the owner and everyone it is shared with see each other live. Your own coding agents show in your room there, as in every office you are a member of.
- **Doors.** Each office has a glowing door, in a gap between the rooms, for every other office sharing connects you to and that you can enter, labelled with whose office it is ("Avery's office") and its environment's name: the offices of environments shared with you, the offices of your own environments that you share (where the people you share them with meet you), and, while you visit someone else's office, a door back to your own (**Your office**). Walk through a door, or click it or its label, to go there. You only ever see doors to offices you can enter.
- **No longer shared.** If the share is revoked while you are in its office, the office says it is no longer shared with you, you leave it at once (everyone else sees you go), and it does not reconnect.
- **Local mode.** Without sign-in, the office opens with just you and your AgentFlow agents, and your own reported agents.

### Chat channels

Use the chip beside the chat box to choose a channel. **Esc** resets it to Nearby. Type `@` to find people in the office and your own agents that can take messages, including live sessions seated at AgentFlow desks. If names overlap, pick the intended recipient from the suggestions. You can also select **Message** from someone's avatar menu.

| Channel | Shortcut | Who gets the message |
|---|---|---|
| **Nearby** (white) | Plain text | People within 6 metres of your avatar get the bubble and log entry. The server checks distance when you send. |
| **Office** (blue) | `/o message` | Everyone in this office gets the bubble and log entry. Flow saves the latest 50 Office messages. |
| **Direct** (purple) | `@Person message` | You and the selected person get the message, and the recipient gets a **Reply** button. When OneProfileID supplies a verified handle and allows you to message that friend, it is saved in [Flow chat](11-chat.md). Otherwise it is relayed within this office as **Office DM: not saved**. Others may see an ellipsis over you. |
| **Agent** (orange) | `@Agent message` | Your selected agent receives it through its reporter. You see the text and replies appear in the agent's transcript as usual. Other people see only that you're talking to an agent. |
| **Office + Agent** | `/o @Agent message` | Two sends: a public Office message and a message to your selected agent. |

Each channel has its own rate limit. Replay records when a message was sent and its channel, without retaining the message text or recipient.

### Day replay

Select **Replay** in the office header and pick a day. Drag the timeline to a time or use **Play** at 1×, 10×, 60× or 300×. The activity graph marks new waits in orange and cards that reached UAT or Done in green. The timeline also shows who was present at the selected time. Replay uses the current office layout. You can still move the camera, and alerts for your live agents appear while you watch. Select **Live** to return to the current office.

Flow keeps up to 14 days of office history. It records agent arrival and departure, running, waiting and idle states, activity kinds, desk assignments and card numbers. It also records when people enter or leave, samples their movement at most once every two seconds, and marks card column moves, emotes, Allow or Deny decisions, and the channel of a sent chat message. Busy offices keep fewer movement samples so the log stays bounded.

The history stores no prompts, transcripts, agent messages or chat text. Only office members can read it. When you open a day, Flow uses your current access to decide which desks and cards you can see. Private agents show as mascots with their status and activity kind, as in the live office. Revoking a share also ends access to the recording through that share.

### Office controls

Open **?** in the office header for the control list and the option to turn off automatic recentering.

| Action | Control |
|---|---|
| Walk | **WASD**, arrow keys, or click/tap a destination |
| Sprint | Hold **Shift** or double-tap and hold a direction |
| Jump | **Space**. Hold for a higher jump. Press again in the air to flip. |
| Orbit | Drag with the middle or right mouse button, **Alt** + left drag, **Q** / **E**, or one-finger drag |
| Zoom | Scroll, use the **+** / **−** buttons, or pinch |
| Pan | Drag with two fingers |
| Recenter | Middle-click or press **F** |
| Top-down overview | Press **O** or select the overview button |
| Edit your look | Press **L**, select the shirt button, click yourself, or press **E** at the mirror in your room or on yourself |
| Gamepad | Left stick to walk, right stick to orbit, **A** to jump, **B** or **X** to sprint |
| Mute / unmute | **M**, or the mic button in the voice bar |
| Push to talk | Hold **V** (turn it on in the voice bar's settings) |
| Meter details | Walk up to a meter and press **E**. **E** opens it only while you are next to it; elsewhere **E** is the usual interact |

### Voice

The meeting room is in the classic office; on the yacht, **Talk to people nearby** works but there is no meeting room yet. The voice bar sits at the bottom right of the office. Its button walks you to the meeting room, and **Talk to people nearby** turns proximity voice on for this visit. While you are in a call it shows where you are and how many people are connected. It also has:

- **The mic button.** It shows whether you are heard: **Mic on** (green), **Muted** (red), **Hold V to talk**, or **Listening only** when the browser was refused the microphone. Click it or press **M**.
- **Deafen.** You hear nobody, and nobody hears you.
- **Share screen.** Shown in the meeting room only.
- **Settings.** Pick a microphone and, where the browser can, a speaker. Turn on push to talk (hold **V**). These choices are kept in this browser.

Keyboard shortcuts never fire while you type in a text field. When you leave a room or turn proximity voice off, the browser gives the microphone back. If the browser blocks sound until you interact with the page (common on phones), the bar shows **Tap to hear**.

**Do not disturb** keeps you out of proximity calls: nobody is connected to you nearby until you change your status. People in Do not disturb are never connected to you either. Walking into the meeting room is your choice, so the room's call ignores it. All calls end when the office closes or the tab has been hidden for more than two minutes, and pick up again when you come back.

**Privacy.** Audio and video go straight between browsers over WebRTC, end-to-end encrypted with DTLS-SRTP. Flow's server only passes the connection set-up messages between two people in the same office. It never records anything, keeps no media, and does not log those messages. When two browsers cannot reach each other directly, a TURN relay you configure carries the encrypted stream (see [docs/self-hosting.md](../self-hosting.md#voice-and-screen-sharing)). Calls are a mesh, which works well for up to about 8 people in one call.

### Meters

Each room has a small screen beside the door, and the common area has one beside the main board. They show, for that member or for the whole office:

- how many agents are running, and how many are waiting, right now
- cards shipped today: moved to UAT or Done since midnight in your timezone (the browser's)
- points shipped this week: the sum of `actual` on those cards, or `points` when a card has no actual. The week starts on Monday
- a sparkline of how many agents were running over the last 24 hours, sampled on the server once a minute and kept in memory

The office meter also shows how many of your own agents are waiting on you. The screens redraw only when the numbers change. Stand next to one and press **E** to open the same figures in a panel.

The meter adds up today’s tokens and estimated cost for the reported agents you can see. Today starts at midnight in each reporter’s local timezone. The [office bridge](https://github.com/aribradshaw/flow/blob/main/docs/office-bridge.md) reads completed T3 provider turns, Claude Code message usage, and Codex CLI token-count events. Sessions without usable data contribute no usage and unknown models contribute tokens only. When no agent sends a figure, the meter shows “—”. Cost is an API-equivalent list price estimate. Subscription plans may include the usage shown here.

Counts use only what you can already see. A card outside your access is not counted. Another member's private agent adds only to the running and waiting numbers, which are already its public status. Its tokens and cost are not sent to you.

### Status

The header has a status control: **Available**, **Focus**, **Do not disturb** or **Away**, and an optional note of up to 60 characters (for example "on a call"). The choice is kept in this browser, and in the server's memory while this Flow process is running, so a reload keeps it and everyone in the office sees it. A coloured ring and an icon sit on the avatar and the name tag, and on the room's door sign. Green is available, amber is focus, red is do not disturb, and grey is away.

Away is also set on its own after 10 minutes with no input while the tab is hidden, and clears when you come back (the tab is visible again, or you press a key or click). An Away you picked yourself stays until you change it.

While someone is in **Do not disturb**, waiting-agent pings and notifications are held and only the badge shows, until they leave it. That includes the browser notification from **Notify me when agents wait**: the badge on the **3D** button still counts them, and the notifications show when they leave Do not disturb. Activity code checks `status.isQuiet(userId)` from `public/office-status.js` before it pings. `userId` is the office member key. When that is true, call `status.notePing(userId, ping)` instead of announcing; it returns `{held: true, count}`. `status.takeHeld(userId)` returns what was held once they leave. The same check on the server is `officeHub.isQuiet(userId)`, and there `userId` may be the member key or the person's email. Pings the office already knows about (an agent that starts waiting) go through this hook on their own.

### Knocking

Each room has a door at its entrance (a themed office can place that door by answering `doorAnchor(room)` with a world position; otherwise it sits in the doorway). The door stops you until it is open. It is taller than a jump, so the way in is the door. On a raised deck the door still stands on that deck. These are room doors. The glowing doors between offices are separate: those are [Doors](#3d-office) to another environment.

Your own room is always open. So is a room whose owner is not in the office, and a room whose owner is **Available** or **Away**: you walk in, and if they are here they hear a soft chime and see "Joe came in".

**Focus** stops you at the door with a Knock prompt (**E**, or the button). Knocking tells only them, with a knock sound and **Let in** / **Not now**. Let in opens that door for 2 minutes. Not now tells you "Joe is focusing". **Do not disturb** is the same door, with no sound for them and only a badge ("2 knocks", or "1 knock") until they leave Do not disturb, when the knocks show. Not now then says they do not want to be disturbed.

A knock is one per 10 seconds between the same two people. Letting someone in, turning them away, and the "came in" notice go only to those two, and only in that office.

### Worlds

An environment's office is drawn as one of two worlds. Everyone who enters sees the same one.

- **Office** (the default). Rooms in a ring on one floor, with the common area in the middle.
- **Yacht.** A superyacht under way at sea. The AgentFlow org stands in the sunken seating of the main-deck lounge, with the main board on the wall ahead of it. Stairs lead up to the upper deck, where each member has a cabin with their name at the door and their board on its back wall. The environment's owner has the bridge at the front. Above the cabins is the sundeck with a pool and a bar, forward of the bridge is the helipad, and at the stern steps go down to the swim platform, where doors to other offices stand. Rails keep you on board unless you jump them. Jump a rail or walk off the swim platform's open end and you fall in with a splash, then come back on the nearest deck.

To change the world, open the office of your own environment and pick **Office** or **Yacht** in the menu beside the environment's name. The choice is saved with the environment (in its AgentFlow data, as `office.world`), so it syncs like any other edit and applies to everyone, within about 15 seconds for people already inside. When you visit a shared environment's office you see the world its owner picked, and the menu is hidden.

The yacht's deck sways a little. **Sea motion** in the controls panel (**?**) turns that off; it starts off when your system asks for reduced motion. The setting is kept in this browser.

The yacht's decks are terraced and never stacked, so each spot has exactly one floor height and everyone agrees where a person stands.

### Your look

Press **L**, use the shirt button in the header, click your own avatar, or walk up to the mirror by the door of your room and press **E**. Standing still for a moment with nothing else in reach offers **E** on yourself too. The editor fills the screen, with you on a turntable: drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom in to your face. Walking pauses while it is open.

Each tab is one part of you, with every choice shown as a small picture of you wearing it:

| Tab | Choices |
| --- | --- |
| Body | Skin tone (twelve tones, or any colour), build and height |
| Face | Eyes and eye colour, eyebrows, nose, mouth, facial hair, glasses, freckles and blush |
| Hair | Twelve styles, from buzz cut to braids, and a colour |
| Hat | Cap, beanie, bucket hat, captain's hat or headphones, and a colour |
| Top | T-shirt, hoodie, button-up, blazer, sweater or tank top, with a colour and an optional pattern in an accent colour |
| Bottoms | Jeans, chinos, shorts, skirt or joggers, and a colour |
| Shoes | Sneakers, boots, loafers or sandals, and a colour |

**Randomize** tries a new look, **Undo** steps back (also Ctrl or Cmd+Z), and **Reset to default** returns to the look picked for you. The buttons under the preview play a walk, a run and the four emotes. Nothing changes for anyone else until you press **Save**; then everyone in the office sees it at once.

Your look belongs to you, not to one office: it follows you into every office you are in, and it is saved on the server (in Postgres, or under `BACKUP_DIR`), so it survives a restart. Only you can change it. The server accepts only the listed choices and plain colours, and keeps colours from being pure black or pure white so a face stays readable.

People blink, look around, shift their weight and fidget while they stand, swing their arms when they walk or run, and move their mouth while their speech bubble shows. Each emote has its own face: a wink with the thumbs up, closed smiling eyes with a clap, a blush with the heart.

### Who sees what

Agents belong to a person, not to an environment: they show in the office of every environment that person is a member of. For each viewer, Flow decides on the server what leaves it:

| Viewer | Sees |
|---|---|
| The agent's owner | Everything, plus Allow / Deny, its transcript, and Send to agent and Stop |
| Someone who can see the Flow project the agent's repo belongs to | Everything except the buttons and the transcript: title, model, machine, repo, project, activity, subagents and the prompt |
| Anyone else | Only the mascot, the vendor and running / waiting / idle, labelled **Private project** |

The environment's owner (and anyone else who can read the whole environment) sees all its projects. A share's recipient sees the projects in their share's scope; a whole-environment share means all of them. An agent whose repo is in none of the environment's projects is private to everyone but its owner, including the environment's owner. Nothing about a private agent (its title, activity, repo, model, prompt, machine, model use or id) is sent to that viewer's browser. A share's recipient also sees only the AgentFlow agents linked to the projects they can see.

A session seated at an AgentFlow agent's desk follows the same rules, with one more: someone other than its owner sees it in full only when they can also see that agent or its card. Otherwise it is a private mascot at its owner's room, and nothing about the seat (the agent, the card) is sent. A desk's queue and finished cards list only the cards the viewer can see.

### Seats

A live session is seated at an AgentFlow agent's desk when Flow can tell which agent and card it works on. This is worked out on the server, in each environment, against that environment's own agents and cards: a session belongs to a person and shows in every office they are a member of, and where the agent is not there it keeps its own desk.

1. **The reporter says so**: `agentflow: {agent, card}` on the agent in the report. `agent` is the AgentFlow agent's id or name; `card` is the card's number (`12` or `"#12"`) or id. With only a card, the agent is the one that card is delegated to, when there is exactly one. An agent this environment does not have means no seat.
2. **The agent runner's title**: `[Flow] <Agent>: #<n> <card title>`, as `tools/agent-runner.mjs` names its threads (an agent's name may hold a colon; a name over 80 characters is cut, and still matches). An agent this environment does not have means no seat.
3. **A card number in the title**: the first `#<n>`.
